SQL.explanation: SQL is the standard language for querying and managing structured relational databases
points: Declarative language — you describe what data you want, not how to get it
Standardized by ANSI/ISO with versions (SQL-92, SQL:1999, SQL:2016) and vendor extensions
Core operations: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, plus DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP)
Powers 80%+ of enterprise data storage worldwide (Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL)
Foundation skill for data analysts, backend developers, data engineers, and BI professionals

NoSQL.explanation: NoSQL databases store unstructured or semi-structured data with flexible scalable schemas
points: Four main families: key-value (Redis), document (MongoDB), column-family (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j)
Designed for horizontal scaling across many servers (scale-out vs scale-up)
Sacrifices some ACID guarantees for BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency)
Ideal for high-write throughput, big data, real-time apps, content management, IoT
Often used alongside relational databases in polyglot persistence architectures

PostgreSQL.explanation: PostgreSQL is a powerful open-source relational database used by millions of applications
points: Fully ACID compliant with advanced features: JSONB, full-text search, geospatial (PostGIS)
MVCC implementation avoids read-write blocking — excellent for concurrent workloads
Extensible via custom functions, operators, data types, and foreign data wrappers
Strong community and ecosystem (TimescaleDB, Citus for scaling, PostgREST for APIs)
Often called the most advanced open-source RDBMS — preferred for complex applications

MongoDB.explanation: MongoDB stores data as JSON documents — great for flexible rapidly changing data structures
points: Document model maps naturally to objects in JavaScript, Python, Java, etc.
Horizontal scaling via sharding + replica sets for high availability
Aggregation framework provides powerful data processing pipeline (like SQL GROUP BY + more)
Atlas managed cloud service dominates modern deployments
Best for content management, catalogs, real-time analytics, mobile backends

Redis.explanation: Redis is an in-memory database used for caching, sessions, and real-time applications
points: Data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, streams, geospatial
Sub-millisecond latency even at millions of operations per second
Persistence options: RDB snapshots and AOF (append-only file) logs
Redis Stack adds JSON, time series, graph, probabilistic data structures
Powers leaderboards, pub/sub messaging, rate limiting, session stores worldwide

Vector DB.explanation: Vector databases like Pinecone and Chroma store AI embeddings for fast similarity search
points: Optimized for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search on high-dimensional vectors
Common indexes: HNSW, IVF, PQ, DiskANN, ScaNN
Critical for semantic search, recommendation systems, RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
Hybrid search combines vector similarity with keyword/metadata filtering
Rapidly growing category with Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Qdrant, Chroma leading

ACID.explanation: ACID ensures database transactions are Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, and Durable
points: Atomicity — all or nothing (via rollback or commit)
Consistency — moves database from one valid state to another (constraints, triggers)
Isolation — concurrent transactions do not interfere (via locking or MVCC)
Durability — committed changes survive crashes (via WAL or similar)
Traditional relational databases guarantee full ACID; many NoSQL offer partial or tunable ACID

Indexing.explanation: Database indexes dramatically speed up queries by creating shortcuts to find data fast
points: B-tree indexes most common for equality and range queries
Composite indexes speed multi-column WHERE clauses and JOINs
Covering indexes can satisfy query entirely from index (index-only scan)
Trade-off: indexes speed reads but slow writes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE)
Over-indexing wastes storage and slows writes — monitor with pg_stat_user_indexes

Graph Database.explanation: Graph databases like Neo4j model and query complex relationships between data points
points: Nodes (entities), relationships (edges), properties on both
Native graph storage & traversal far faster than relational JOINs for deep connections
Cypher (Neo4j), Gremlin, SPARQL common query languages
Ideal for social networks, fraud detection, recommendation engines, knowledge graphs
Often combined with vector search in modern AI applications

Sharding.explanation: Sharding splits a database across multiple servers to handle massive scale and traffic
points: Horizontal partitioning by key (user_id, region, tenant_id)
Challenges: cross-shard queries, rebalancing, hot shards
MongoDB, Cassandra, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB built for automatic sharding
Application-level sharding still common for custom requirements
Essential for systems exceeding single-node capacity (Instagram, Uber, Discord)

Replication.explanation: Replication copies data across multiple servers so your database stays up if one server fails
points: Master-slave (primary-replica) most common pattern
Synchronous vs asynchronous replication trade consistency vs performance
Multi-master / active-active for global applications
Used for high availability, read scaling, geographic distribution
Failover automation critical (Patroni, Orchestrator, built-in cluster managers)

Primary Key.explanation: A primary key is a unique identifier that distinguishes each row in a database table
points: Must be unique and NOT NULL
Usually single column (surrogate key) or composite
Automatically creates unique index
Referenced by foreign keys in other tables
Choosing good PK affects performance, storage, and query patterns

Foreign Key.explanation: A foreign key links rows in one table to rows in another creating a relationship
points: Enforces referential integrity (prevents orphan records)
Can be NULL unless explicitly NOT NULL
Supports ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT, NO ACTION
Can create performance overhead on writes
Essential for relational data modeling and data consistency

JOIN.explanation: A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables based on a matching column value
points: INNER JOIN (most common), LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER JOIN, CROSS JOIN
Equi-join (ON col = col) vs non-equi (>, <, BETWEEN)
Hash join, merge join, nested loop join algorithms used by optimizer
Multi-table joins can explode in cost — index and filter early
Modern databases push down predicates and reorder joins for performance

INNER JOIN.explanation: INNER JOIN returns only the rows where a match exists in both joined tables
points: Most frequently used join type
Equivalent to WHERE clause with equality condition (old syntax)
Can be expensive without proper indexes on join columns
Multiple INNER JOINs common in normalized schemas
Optimizer often rewrites to hash or merge join for large tables

LEFT JOIN.explanation: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right
points: Preserves all records from primary (left) table
RIGHT JOIN is mirror image (less commonly used)
Common for finding missing related records (IS NULL pattern)
Can produce many NULLs — affects aggregates and filters
Performance similar to INNER JOIN when right table is indexed

Index Scan.explanation: An index scan uses a database index to find rows quickly without scanning every row
points: Index-only scan possible when all needed columns are in index
Bitmap index scan combines multiple indexes efficiently
Index range scan for >, <, BETWEEN conditions
Much faster than table scan on large tables
EXPLAIN shows whether index is used and expected cost

Full Table Scan.explanation: A full table scan reads every row in a table which is slow on large datasets
points: Occurs when no suitable index exists or query is non-selective
Parallel sequential scan in modern databases reduces time
Avoid on tables > few million rows unless tiny fraction returned
Common in small tables or when optimizer estimates full scan is faster
High I/O cost — primary cause of slow queries

Query Planner.explanation: The query planner figures out the most efficient way to execute a SQL query
points: Uses statistics (pg_statistic) to estimate row counts and costs
Generates multiple possible plans and chooses lowest-cost one
Can be influenced by indexes, constraints, explicit JOIN order
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows actual vs estimated costs
Bad statistics or correlations lead to poor plan choices

Normalization.explanation: Normalization organizes a database to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity
points: 1NF → atomic values, 2NF → no partial dependencies, 3NF → no transitive dependencies
Boyce-Codd NF (BCNF) stronger than 3NF for certain cases
Reduces update anomalies and storage waste
Over-normalization can hurt read performance due to many JOINs
Most production databases aim for 3NF or BCNF

Denormalization.explanation: Denormalization adds redundancy to a database to speed up read-heavy query performance
points: Common in data warehouses and read-heavy OLAP systems
Materialized views, redundant columns, pre-joined tables
Increases write complexity and storage usage
Used when read performance is more critical than write cost
Modern systems often combine normalized OLTP + denormalized OLAP

Schema.explanation: A database schema defines the structure, tables, columns, and data types of a database
points: Logical schema (tables, columns, constraints) vs physical (indexes, partitioning)
Public schema default in PostgreSQL, dbo in SQL Server
Multi-tenant systems often use schema-per-tenant pattern
Schema migrations managed by Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, Prisma
Good schema design prevents data anomalies and improves performance

Migration.explanation: Database migrations manage version-controlled changes to a database schema over time
points: Up migrations (apply changes) and down migrations (rollback)
Tools: Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, Django migrations, Prisma Migrate
Zero-downtime strategies: add column nullable first, backfill, then NOT NULL
Critical for continuous deployment in production
Schema drift detection prevents surprises

ORM.explanation: Object-Relational Mapping lets developers interact with databases using code objects instead of SQL
points: Popular libraries: SQLAlchemy (Python), Hibernate (Java), Entity Framework (.NET), Prisma (TS)
Reduces boilerplate but can hide performance issues
N+1 problem common when not using eager loading / joins
Great for rapid development and simple CRUD
Many teams use lightweight ORMs or raw SQL for complex queries

Stored Procedure.explanation: Stored procedures are pre-compiled SQL logic saved in the database for reuse and speed
points: Executed on database server — less network round-trips
Can include business logic, transactions, error handling
Parameters (IN, OUT, INOUT) and return values
Security benefit: execute permission without table access
Less popular in modern microservices (favor services layer)

Trigger.explanation: A database trigger automatically runs code when a specified event like insert or update occurs
points: Row-level vs statement-level triggers
BEFORE, AFTER, INSTEAD OF timing
Common uses: audit logging, validation, maintaining derived columns
Can cause performance overhead and debugging difficulty
Use sparingly — business logic usually better in application layer

View.explanation: A database view is a saved query that acts like a virtual table for simpler querying
points: Does not store data — query runs every time view is accessed
Simplifies complex queries, hides implementation details
Updatable views in some cases (simple single-table views)
Materialized views store results for performance
Security feature: grant access to view, not underlying tables

Materialized View.explanation: A materialized view caches the results of a query on disk for much faster reads
points: PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server support natively
REFRESH COMPLETE or incremental (some systems)
Great for expensive aggregations, reporting, dashboards
Trade-off: storage cost and refresh latency
TimescaleDB continuous aggregates automate incremental refresh

Partition.explanation: Partitioning divides a large table into smaller pieces to improve query and management performance
points: Range, list, hash partitioning strategies
Partition pruning eliminates irrelevant partitions from query
Faster bulk loads, deletes, index maintenance
PostgreSQL declarative partitioning (10+) very powerful
Essential for tables > hundreds of GB or billions of rows

B-tree Index.explanation: B-tree indexes are balanced tree structures ideal for range queries and equality lookups
points: Default index type in PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server
Excellent for =, <, >, BETWEEN, IN, ORDER BY
Self-balancing — O(log n) search time
Supports multi-column (composite) indexes
Can become bloated — needs periodic REINDEX or VACUUM

Hash Index.explanation: Hash indexes provide O(1) lookup speed for exact equality queries
points: PostgreSQL hash indexes improved significantly since version 10
Only for equality (=) — no range or ordering
Smaller than B-tree for some data distributions
Not suited for frequently updated tables (hash collisions)
Useful for very high-cardinality equality lookups

GiST Index.explanation: GiST indexes in PostgreSQL support complex data types like geographic and full-text search
points: Generalized Search Tree — lossy index for geometric, full-text, custom types
Used by PostGIS for spatial queries (contains, within, nearest)
Supports operator classes for different data types
Balances speed vs accuracy (tunable)
Essential for GIS, similarity search, text search applications

Full-text Search.explanation: Full-text search indexes words in documents to enable fast natural language text queries
points: PostgreSQL tsvector/tsquery powerful built-in FTS
Ranking, stemming, stop words, dictionaries, thesaurus
GIN or GiST index types for performance
Hybrid search combines FTS with vector similarity
Elasticsearch/OpenSearch often used for advanced search needs

Transaction.explanation: A transaction is a group of database operations that all succeed or all fail together
points: BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK syntax
Isolation levels control visibility of concurrent changes
Savepoints allow partial rollback within transaction
Distributed transactions (XA/2PC) for multiple databases
Long-running transactions hurt concurrency — keep short

Rollback.explanation: Rollback undoes all changes in a transaction if something goes wrong
points: Automatic on connection close without COMMIT
Uses WAL (write-ahead log) to reconstruct previous state
Can be very expensive for large transactions
Savepoints allow nested rollback points
Critical for data integrity in error conditions

Commit.explanation: Commit saves all changes in a transaction permanently to the database
points: Durability guaranteed after commit (fsync or equivalent)
Two-phase commit in distributed systems
Write-ahead logging ensures crash recovery
Triggers and constraints checked at commit time
Point of no return — changes become visible to others

Deadlock.explanation: A deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs to proceed
points: Database detects and aborts one transaction automatically
Prevention: consistent lock ordering, short transactions
Detection via wait-for graph
Common in high-concurrency UPDATE/DELETE patterns
Logging and monitoring deadlocks important for troubleshooting

Isolation Level.explanation: Isolation levels control how much one transaction can see the uncommitted data of another
points: Read Uncommitted → dirty reads possible
Read Committed → no dirty reads (default in most DBs)
Repeatable Read → no non-repeatable reads
Serializable → no phantom reads, strongest isolation
PostgreSQL uses MVCC — no read locks at Repeatable Read

WAL.explanation: Write-Ahead Logging records changes before applying them ensuring durability and crash recovery
points: Core durability mechanism in PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server
Redo logs allow replay after crash
Checkpoint process flushes dirty pages to data files
WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery
WAL size and checkpoint tuning affect performance

MVCC.explanation: Multi-Version Concurrency Control lets readers and writers work simultaneously without blocking each other
points: PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server use MVCC
Each row version has xmin/xmax transaction IDs
Readers see consistent snapshot from their transaction start
No read locks — excellent for read-heavy workloads
Vacuum/autovacuum cleans up dead tuples

Connection Pool.explanation: A connection pool reuses database connections to avoid the overhead of opening new ones
points: Popular libraries: PgBouncer, HikariCP, SQLAlchemy pool, c3p0
Reduces connection establishment latency and resource usage
Max pool size, min idle, timeout settings critical
Connection leaks cause pool exhaustion — monitor carefully
Essential for high-concurrency applications

ORM N+1 Problem.explanation: The N+1 problem is when an ORM executes one query per row instead of joining efficiently
points: Classic example: load users → then loop and load each user's posts
Solution: eager loading, join fetching, batch fetching
Can turn O(1) query into O(N) queries — disastrous at scale
Use EXPLAIN to detect
Many ORMs now warn or auto-optimize N+1 patterns

Cassandra.explanation: Apache Cassandra is a distributed NoSQL database designed for massive write throughput
points: Masterless architecture — every node equal
Linear scalability and tunable consistency
Wide-column model with CQL (SQL-like) query language
Used by Apple, Netflix, Uber, Discord at extreme scale
Excellent for time-series, IoT, messaging, high-write workloads

DynamoDB.explanation: DynamoDB is AWS's managed NoSQL database offering single-digit millisecond latency at any scale
points: Fully managed — no servers, automatic scaling
Provisioned or on-demand capacity modes
Global tables for multi-region replication
DAX in-memory cache for microsecond reads
Powers Amazon.com shopping cart, Alexa, many AWS services

MySQL.explanation: MySQL is the world's most widely used open-source relational database powering countless websites
points: InnoDB default engine with full ACID and foreign keys
Very fast for read-heavy workloads
Replication and Group Replication for HA
PlanetScale, Vitess, AWS Aurora MySQL variants
Still dominant for web applications (WordPress, Drupal, etc.)

SQLite.explanation: SQLite is a serverless embedded database that stores everything in a single file
points: Zero-configuration — no server process needed
Used in billions of mobile devices, browsers, IoT
ACID compliant with WAL mode
DuckDB and libSQL extend SQLite for analytics and distributed use
Perfect for local-first apps, testing, small websites

MariaDB.explanation: MariaDB is a community-driven MySQL fork with additional features and performance improvements
points: Drop-in replacement for MySQL
Aria, ColumnStore, Spider, Sequence engines
Better optimizer and query cache in some cases
Temporal tables, system-versioned tables
Strong community after Oracle acquired MySQL

Oracle DB.explanation: Oracle Database is the dominant enterprise relational database trusted by large corporations
points: Exadata engineered system for extreme performance
Advanced partitioning, RAC, Data Guard, GoldenGate
PL/SQL powerful procedural language
Autonomous Database (cloud) automates tuning and scaling
Still runs many Fortune 500 core systems

Microsoft SQL Server.explanation: SQL Server is Microsoft's enterprise database tightly integrated with the Windows ecosystem
points: T-SQL dialect with powerful procedural features
Always On Availability Groups for HA
Columnstore indexes for analytics
Azure SQL Database managed service
Strong in business intelligence (SSRS, SSIS, SSAS)

Snowflake.explanation: Snowflake is a cloud data warehouse that separates compute and storage for flexible scaling
points: Virtual warehouses scale compute independently of storage
Time travel and zero-copy cloning features
Snowpipe for continuous loading
Multi-cloud support (AWS, Azure, GCP)
Rapidly becoming standard for modern analytics

BigQuery.explanation: BigQuery is Google's serverless data warehouse for analyzing massive datasets with SQL
points: Columnar storage and Dremel query engine
Pay-per-query pricing (on-demand) or flat-rate slots
BI Engine for sub-second dashboards
Integration with Looker, Data Studio, Vertex AI
Federated queries to external sources

Redshift.explanation: Amazon Redshift is a cloud data warehouse optimized for analytical queries on large datasets
points: Columnar storage and massively parallel processing
Redshift Spectrum queries data in S3 without loading
Concurrency scaling and elastic resize
AQUA (hardware acceleration) for faster queries
Strong integration with AWS ecosystem

ClickHouse.explanation: ClickHouse is an extremely fast columnar database built for real-time analytics
points: Designed for OLAP — aggregates billions of rows per second
MergeTree family of table engines
Vectorized query execution and compression
Used by Cloudflare, Lyft, Cisco, eBay
Open-source with excellent performance/price ratio

DuckDB.explanation: DuckDB is an in-process analytical database that runs fast SQL queries on local files
points: Zero server — embedded like SQLite but for analytics
Columnar-vectorized execution engine
Parquet, CSV, JSON direct querying
Excellent Python/ R integration (pandas-like)
Rapidly replacing pandas for large local datasets

InfluxDB.explanation: InfluxDB is a purpose-built time series database for metrics, monitoring, and IoT data
points: Flux query language (newer) and InfluxQL
High cardinality support improved in 2.x
Telegraf agent for easy collection
Used for DevOps monitoring, IoT, real-time analytics
InfluxDB Cloud and Enterprise offerings

TimescaleDB.explanation: TimescaleDB extends PostgreSQL with time-series capabilities for fast time-ordered data
points: Hypertables automatically partition by time
Continuous aggregates for real-time rollups
Compression reduces storage 90%+
Full PostgreSQL features + time-series optimizations
Popular for monitoring, IoT, financial data

CockroachDB.explanation: CockroachDB is a distributed SQL database that survives regional failures automatically
points: PostgreSQL wire-compatible
Geo-partitioning and multi-region capabilities
Automatic rebalancing and repair
Strong consistency with serializable isolation
Cloud-native with managed CockroachCloud

PlanetScale.explanation: PlanetScale is a MySQL-compatible serverless database platform with branching like Git
points: Vitess under the hood for horizontal scaling
Schema changes non-blocking with online DDL
Database branching for safe experimentation
Boost for query acceleration
Focus on developer experience and safety

Supabase.explanation: Supabase is an open-source Firebase alternative built on PostgreSQL with real-time features
points: PostgreSQL + real-time subscriptions via LISTEN/NOTIFY
Built-in auth, storage, edge functions
Auto-generated REST/GraphQL APIs
Growing rapidly among indie developers
Open-source self-hosting option

Firebase.explanation: Firebase is Google's real-time NoSQL cloud database popular for mobile and web apps
points: Realtime Database (JSON) and Firestore (document)
Offline persistence and sync
Authentication, Cloud Functions, Hosting, Storage
Strong mobile SDKs (iOS, Android, Flutter)
Pay-as-you-go pricing can become expensive at scale

Firestore.explanation: Firestore is Google's flexible scalable NoSQL cloud database with offline support
points: Document-collection model with subcollections
Powerful real-time listeners
Offline persistence and automatic sync
Scales automatically to millions of users
Integration with Firebase Authentication and Functions

Fauna.explanation: Fauna is a serverless transactional database with a document-relational data model
points: Global distribution with strong consistency
Temporal queries and history tracking
FQL query language (functional)
ACID transactions across regions
Used by Verizon Media, Wealthfront, TripActions

Couchbase.explanation: Couchbase combines NoSQL flexibility with SQL query support and built-in caching
points: Key-value + document model
N1QL SQL-like query language
Built-in distributed cache (like Memcached)
Cross Datacenter Replication (XDCR)
Used by eBay, LinkedIn, Marriott, Vodafone

Elasticsearch.explanation: Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene
points: Inverted index for full-text search
Distributed by design — scales horizontally
Kibana for visualization, Logstash/Beats for ingestion
ELK stack dominant for logging and monitoring
OpenSearch fork after Elastic license change

OpenSearch.explanation: OpenSearch is AWS's open-source fork of Elasticsearch for search and log analytics
points: Maintained by AWS and community
Feature parity with Elasticsearch 7.10 + new features
OpenSearch Dashboards (Kibana fork)
Security Analytics, Anomaly Detection, Neural search
Strong AWS integration and managed service

Apache Solr.explanation: Solr is an enterprise search platform built on Lucene with rich faceting and filtering
points: Mature, stable enterprise search engine
Powerful faceting, grouping, highlighting
SolrCloud for distributed deployment
Used by Netflix, eBay, Disney, Apple
Strong in e-commerce and content search

Neo4j.explanation: Neo4j is the leading graph database using nodes and edges to model complex relationships
points: Cypher query language very readable
ACID transactions and high availability
Graph Data Science library for algorithms
Bloom visualization tool
Used for fraud detection, recommendation, knowledge graphs

Amazon Neptune.explanation: Neptune is AWS's managed graph database supporting both property graph and RDF queries
points: Gremlin (property graph) and SPARQL (RDF) support
Multi-AZ high availability
Fast parallel loading from S3
Integration with AWS ecosystem
Used for knowledge graphs, fraud, recommendation

ArangoDB.explanation: ArangoDB is a multi-model database supporting graphs, documents, and key-value in one system
points: AQL query language unifies models
Native graph support with traversals
Foxx microservices framework
SatelliteCollections for low-latency reads
Good for complex, mixed workloads

Dgraph.explanation: Dgraph is a distributed graph database that uses GraphQL as its native query language
points: GraphQL± query language
Horizontal scalability with sharding
ACID transactions
Full-text search and geo support
Strong focus on developer experience

Memcached.explanation: Memcached is a simple high-performance distributed memory cache for speeding up web apps
points: Key-value store in RAM only
Very fast — sub-millisecond gets/sets
No persistence or replication
Multi-threaded since 1.6
Still widely used for simple caching

Apache HBase.explanation: HBase is a Hadoop-based NoSQL database for random real-time access to big data
points: Modeled after Google BigTable
Runs on HDFS with strong consistency
Column-family model
Used by Facebook, Adobe, Yahoo for big data
Phoenix provides SQL layer

Apache Hive.explanation: Hive is a data warehouse built on Hadoop enabling SQL queries over distributed storage
points: HiveQL → MapReduce/Tez/Spark execution
Schema-on-read approach
ACID support since Hive 1.0
Used for batch ETL and analytics on Hadoop
Being supplemented by Spark SQL and Presto

Apache Spark SQL.explanation: Spark SQL runs SQL queries over massive distributed datasets using Apache Spark
points: Catalyst optimizer and Tungsten execution engine
DataFrame/Dataset API + SQL
Hive metastore compatibility
Works with Parquet, Delta Lake, Iceberg
Dominant for big data processing

Presto.explanation: Presto is a distributed SQL query engine for running fast queries across heterogeneous data sources
points: Federated queries — no data movement
Connectors for Hive, Cassandra, Kafka, PostgreSQL, etc.
Trino fork (formerly PrestoSQL) most active
Very fast ad-hoc analytics
Used by Facebook, Uber, Netflix, Airbnb

Apache Iceberg.explanation: Iceberg is an open table format for huge analytics tables with ACID transactions
points: Schema evolution, partitioning evolution, time travel
Works with Spark, Flink, Trino, Hive, Impala
Hidden partitioning avoids query rewrite
Snapshot isolation and rollback
Rapidly becoming de-facto lakehouse table format

Delta Lake.explanation: Delta Lake adds ACID transactions and versioning to data lakes stored on cloud storage
points: Open-source storage layer on Parquet
ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel
Optimized for Spark but works with others
Z-order clustering and data skipping
Strong adoption in Databricks ecosystem

Apache Parquet.explanation: Parquet is a columnar storage format that compresses analytical data efficiently
points: Columnar storage → great compression and column pruning
Predicate pushdown and projection
Nested data support
Standard for data lakes (Iceberg, Delta, Hudi)
10×–100× faster analytics than row formats

Data Lake.explanation: A data lake stores raw structured and unstructured data at massive scale for later analysis
points: Schema-on-read approach — load first, structure later
Usually on cheap object storage (S3, ADLS, GCS)
Supports big data tools (Spark, Presto, Hive)
Governance and quality challenges common
Evolving to lakehouse with table formats

Data Warehouse.explanation: A data warehouse stores structured historical data optimized for business intelligence queries
points: Schema-on-write → clean, structured data
Star/snowflake schemas common
Optimized for aggregations and reporting
Traditional: Teradata, Oracle, Netezza; Cloud: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift
Usually loaded via ETL processes

Lakehouse.explanation: A lakehouse combines data lake flexibility with data warehouse analytics performance
points: Uses open table formats (Iceberg, Delta, Hudi)
ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel
Directly queryable with Spark, Presto, Trino
Eliminates data silos between lake and warehouse
Databricks, Snowflake, Dremio leading implementations

ETL.explanation: Extract Transform Load moves data from source systems into a warehouse in a structured form
points: Traditional pattern for data warehousing
Tools: Informatica, Talend, Matillion, dbt (ELT variant)
Batch-oriented — daily/ hourly runs
Transformations happen before loading
Being supplemented by ELT in cloud era

ELT.explanation: ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse using its compute power
points: Leverages cloud data warehouse scale for transformations
Tools: dbt, Snowflake Snowpark, BigQuery scripts
Faster iteration, better handling of raw data
Enables data lakehouse patterns
Modern default for cloud analytics

Change Data Capture.explanation: CDC tracks every insert, update, and delete in a database and streams changes in real time
points: Debezium leading open-source CDC platform
Kafka Connect integration common
Supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB
Enables real-time data pipelines, replication, analytics
Critical for event-driven architectures

Database Cursor.explanation: A cursor iterates over query results one row at a time instead of loading all at once
points: Used for processing large result sets without memory explosion
DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH, CLOSE syntax
Scrollable vs forward-only cursors
Server-side vs client-side cursors
Performance overhead — avoid when possible

Explain Plan.explanation: EXPLAIN shows exactly how a database intends to execute a query for optimization
points: EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs query and shows real timings
Node types: Seq Scan, Index Scan, Hash Join, etc.
Cost estimates help identify bottlenecks
PostgreSQL EXPLAIN has many format options (JSON, YAML)
Essential skill for query optimization

Query Cache.explanation: Query caching saves results of expensive queries so identical requests return instantly
points: MySQL query cache (removed in 8.0)
PostgreSQL prepared statements + plan caching
Application-level caching (Redis) more common
Invalidation difficult — time-based or write-through
Edge caching (Varnish, CDN) for HTTP responses

Optimistic Locking.explanation: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare and only checks for them at commit time
points: Version column or timestamp checked on update
UPDATE ... WHERE version = old_version
Throws exception on conflict → retry logic
Better concurrency than pessimistic locking
Common in web applications and ORMs

Pessimistic Locking.explanation: Pessimistic locking locks data as soon as it is accessed to prevent any concurrent modification
points: SELECT FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE
Row-level or table-level locks
Can cause contention and deadlocks
Used when conflicts are likely or data critical
Long locks hurt scalability — use carefully

Two-phase Commit.explanation: 2PC ensures all nodes in a distributed transaction either all commit or all rollback together
points: Prepare phase → commit phase
XA standard for Java and databases
Coordinator failure can cause blocking
Performance overhead and complexity
Modern systems prefer eventual consistency or sagas

CAP Theorem.explanation: CAP theorem states a distributed system can only guarantee two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance
points: CP → consistent + partition tolerant (many relational DBs)
AP → available + partition tolerant (Cassandra, DynamoDB)
CA → rare in distributed systems (single node)
Brewer later clarified it's about trade-offs during partitions
Guides architecture decisions in distributed systems

BASE.explanation: BASE databases are Basically Available, Soft-state, and Eventually consistent — the NoSQL alternative to ACID
points: Designed for high availability and partition tolerance
Accepts temporary inconsistency for scalability
Common in distributed NoSQL systems
Eventual consistency models vary (causal, monotonic reads)
Suits many web-scale applications

Eventual Consistency.explanation: Eventual consistency guarantees data will be consistent across nodes eventually but not immediately
points: Tunable consistency in Cassandra, DynamoDB
Read-your-writes, monotonic reads variants
Conflict resolution strategies (last-write-wins, CRDTs)
Critical for globally distributed systems
Acceptable for many use cases (social feeds, shopping carts)

Strong Consistency.explanation: Strong consistency ensures every read immediately reflects the most recent write
points: Linearizability — strongest model
Requires coordination or locking
Higher latency and lower availability during partitions
Traditional relational databases provide this
Used when correctness is paramount (banking, inventory)

Surrogate Key.explanation: A surrogate key is a system-generated unique ID like an auto-increment integer with no business meaning
points: Eliminates natural key changes (email, SSN)
Smaller and faster for indexing and joins
UUIDs vs auto-increment debate (monotonic vs distributed)
Snowflake IDs popular for distributed systems
Most common primary key choice in modern databases

Natural Key.explanation: A natural key uses real-world data like email or SSN as the unique row identifier
points: Business meaning and readability
Risk of changes requiring cascading updates
Composite natural keys common (order_id + line_item)
Can cause performance issues if large strings
Less common as primary key today

Composite Key.explanation: A composite key uses two or more columns together to uniquely identify a row
points: Common in junction tables (many-to-many)
Order of columns matters for index efficiency
Can be natural or surrogate components
Foreign keys referencing composite keys cumbersome
Modern preference for single surrogate PK

Columnstore Index.explanation: Columnstore indexes store data by column for dramatically faster analytical aggregation queries
points: SQL Server, PostgreSQL (cstore_fdw), BigQuery, Snowflake native
Excellent compression and batch processing
Segment elimination skips irrelevant data
Ideal for data warehouse and analytics workloads
Slower for point lookups and OLTP

Bitmap Index.explanation: Bitmap indexes are space-efficient indexes ideal for low-cardinality columns like status flags
points: Each value gets a bitmap of row positions
Excellent for AND/OR combinations
Used in Oracle, PostgreSQL (via extensions)
Very small for low-cardinality data
Updates expensive — best for read-heavy data

Connection String.explanation: A connection string contains host, port, database name, and credentials to connect to a database
points: Format varies by driver (ODBC, JDBC, libpq)
Sensitive information — never commit to git
Use environment variables or secret managers
Connection pooling parameters often included
SSL/TLS options critical for security
